clue.text: Funny hymn about — "Honour Love's Namesake"

indicators.note: about means going round, so the shuffled hymn wraps the other pieces
funny suggests something odd or peculiar, so the letters of hymn are reworked

parts.note: OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A comic hymn celebrates a namesake of Love, title and all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' looks like a comment on the hymn but is the anagram signal; 'about' is the container signal. OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A word spelt or sounded like another is its namesake in the linguistic sense, a pair sharing one name.

clue.text: Dances with music-maker and -others

parts.note: a horn is a musical instrument
pipes are further instruments, other music-makers

explanation.surface: Dancing to music played on one instrument and several more.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash before 'others' is a print oddity.
explanation.definitionFit: Lively solo dances traditionally performed by sailors go by this name.

clue.text: Maize that is ingested in breakfasts, say

indicators.note: ingested in means swallowed into, so the abbreviation goes inside

parts.note: breakfasts are examples of meals
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Maize that gets eaten at breakfast time.
explanation.walkthrough: MEALIES is South African English for maize.
explanation.definitionFit: In southern Africa corn on the cob, or the crop itself, is called by this name.

clue.text: Number one in a quarter, for example

definitions.text: Number one in a quarter, for example

parts.words: Number one in a quarter, for example
parts.note: in the fraction one quarter, the top figure is one, the number above the line

explanation.surface: Who comes first in a city quarter?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' suggests a champion and 'quarter' a district; the clue means the fraction 1/4, whose upper figure is 1.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure above the line of a fraction is named this, as 1 in one quarter.

clue.text: Miss is getting warmer

definitions.meaning: to miss a catch or chance is to bungle it
a fur tube that keeps the hands warm

explanation.surface: A young lady is feeling the heat.
explanation.definitionFit: To bungle a catch is to fumble it, and a fur hand-warmer is the same word.

clue.text: Too hurried — not a success

parts.note: too in the sense of additionally, as well
hurried means ran, past tense of run

explanation.surface: Someone who rushed too much ended up failing.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse or competitor who finishes unplaced, hence a failure.

clue.text: "Cats is mice?" Correct this with severity

indicators.note: correcting the quoted phrase means rearranging its muddled letters

explanation.surface: Someone insists, with a stern tone, that 'cats is mice' be put right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct this' tells you to rearrange the ungrammatical phrase CATS IS MICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-denial and austere living mean harsh discipline, a kind of strictness.

clue.text: Part, by direction, at any time

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south, a direction
ever means at any time

explanation.surface: Separated by orders, whenever that may be.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut off or divide is to separate, as to part company.

clue.text: Up to no good in pop music escapade

indicators.note: in means the reversed word goes inside the word for pop music

parts.note: rock is a kind of popular music

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for no good is read from bottom to top

parts.note: ill means bad, no good

explanation.surface: Misbehaving during a pop concert adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' works because this is a down entry, read bottom to top; 'in' is the container signal. 'Up to no good' looks like one phrase, but 'to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A boisterous frolic or spree is an escapade, and that is the old noun sense of this word.

clue.text: Poor edition held by a Marshal

indicators.note: held by means contained in, so the abbreviation sits inside the name

parts.note: Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: A shabby printing is kept by a military officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Marshal Ney, Napoleon's 'bravest of the brave', is the Marshal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking money or means is being impoverished.

clue.text: Province insecure — almost

annotationWithheld.why: 'Province insecure - almost (5)': REALM runs through insecuRE ALMost, but the only hiding signal is the 'in' of 'insecure', a word that must also supply the letters RE, so one word does two jobs.

clue.text: Faustus put Helen's at 1,000 ships

parts.note: in Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, Helen of Troy is hailed for the looks that launched a thousand ships, so her looks were rated at that worth

explanation.surface: Marlowe's doctor puts a price on Helen of Troy in warships.
explanation.walkthrough: Marlowe's Faustus asks 'Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?' about Helen of Troy; the clue reads that line as a price tag.
explanation.definitionFit: The nominal worth printed on something is its stated price, here what Helen's looks were reckoned at.

clue.text: Paul's about — runs with joyful cry in the monastery

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the surname is put round the other pieces

parts.note: Paul Pry is a nosy busybody from a 19th-century comedy, so Paul's surname is taken
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
io is a Latin and Greek shout of triumph or joy

explanation.surface: A man named Paul goes about with a shout of joy inside a monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Pry, title character of an 1825 comedy, became a byword for a meddler, a figure older solvers would know; 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A religious house governed by a prior is a small monastery or convent.

clue.text: was in our lips and eyes' (A and C.)

definitions.text: was in our lips and eyes

parts.words: was in our lips and eyes
parts.note: a missing first word completes Cleopatra's line in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra

explanation.surface: Fill the gap in a line from Antony and Cleopatra.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue is a quotation with a dash for the missing word; (A. and C.) names Antony and Cleopatra, where Cleopatra says the lovers' parting words: '... was in our lips and eyes, Bliss in our brows' bent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra says endless timelessness lived in their kisses and looks, the word for forever that begins the quoted line.

clue.text: Expedition's last straw, a road restriction!

parts.note: expedition can mean promptness or haste, that is speed
'that's the limit' says the same as 'that's the last straw'

explanation.surface: The final straw on a long trip is a traffic rule!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' suggests a journey but means haste here.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal maximum velocity on a road is a rule restricting drivers.

clue.text: Place, or put one in place

indicators.note: in means the one letter goes inside the word for place

parts.note: to post someone is to place them, as at a station
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: An instruction to position something, or slot one item into its spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put' is a link word; 'in' puts I inside POST.
explanation.definitionFit: To put forward a claim is to set it down as a premise, laying it out as a starting point.

clue.text: With respect to the manufacturer, this can mend a broken heart

definitions.text: this can mend a broken heart

parts.note: pace, from Latin, is used to mean with due respect to someone's opinion
a maker is one who manufactures

explanation.surface: Respectfully, the maker of this device says it can heal heartbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: Pace, said PAY-see or PAH-chay, is a formal Latin word meaning 'with all respect to'. A broken heart is meant medically, not romantically.
explanation.definitionFit: A small implanted electrical device regulates a faulty heartbeat, so it repairs a failing heart.

clue.text: Softened spice is valued

parts.note: mace is a spice made from nutmeg husks
rated means assessed or valued

explanation.surface: Tenderised spice is highly prized.
explanation.definitionFit: Soaked in liquid until soft, as food left to steep.

clue.text: About a tense act

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the present is a grammatical tense

explanation.surface: Concerning an anxious performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' is a link word; 'tense' looks like an adjective but is the grammar noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To act for someone is to stand in for them, speaking on their behalf.

clue.text: Absolute head in Sheppey's place

parts.note: sheer means utter or absolute, as in sheer folly
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: The absolute head of affairs on the Isle of Sheppey.
explanation.walkthrough: SHEERNESS is a port town on the Isle of Sheppey, an island in the Thames estuary in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: The town is the main settlement on that Kentish island, so it is a place there.

clue.text: The error of one recent seducer

indicators.note: error suggests a muddle, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recent mistake by a seducer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' is a link; 'error of' jumbles I and RECENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lures or tempts another is a seducer.

clue.text: Pile of bricks left in temporary quarters

indicators.note: in means the letter for left is put inside the word for temporary quarters

parts.note: a camp is a temporary set of lodgings, of tents or huts

explanation.surface: A heap of bricks abandoned in a makeshift camp.
explanation.walkthrough: A clamp is a stack of unfired bricks built to be fired in place, a little-known sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Brickmakers call a stacked heap of raw bricks for firing by this name.

clue.text: A duck in the East producing a sort of dye

parts.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, nil
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A duck in Asia gives off a coloured stain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is not a container here but its own two letters, IN.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal-tar compound used to make synthetic colouring is one of the dyestuffs.

clue.text: Poor cows — told to be sheep

indicators.note: poor here means badly made, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Unfortunate cows are told they must be sheep from now on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' shuffles COWS and TOLD together.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-woolled breed of ovine animal from the Gloucestershire hills carries this name.

clue.text: Basic military unit died in charge

indicators.note: in means the letter for died is put inside the word for charge

parts.note: care means charge, as in in someone's charge

explanation.surface: A small army unit died while on duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A permanent core of trained soldiers forming a unit's nucleus is called this.

clue.text: Contrive to get a Bible in miniature case

indicators.note: case means an enclosing cover, so the small word encloses the Bible abbreviation

parts.note: wee means tiny, miniature
AV is the Authorised Version of the Bible

explanation.surface: Managing to fit a Bible inside a tiny box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' and 'in' are links; 'case' is the container signal. AV is the Authorised (King James) Version of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: To weave a plot is to devise or concoct it.

clue.text: Railway service in receipt of one pound

parts.note: BR stood for British Rail, the former national railway

indicators.note: in receipt of means receiving, so the word for service takes in the numeral

parts.note: use, as in being of use, is service
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A railway service has received a single pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pound is money; the definition is the verb, to pound or crush.
explanation.definitionFit: To batter something hard enough to damage it is to injure or crush it, as when pounding fruit.

clue.text: Time to get up and put things right

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: tide is an old word for time or season, as in Yuletide

explanation.surface: Time to rise and fix what is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: TIDE is an old word for time, as in Yuletide; 'to get up' turns it to EDIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To revise text and correct errors is to fix it.

clue.text: Recited — by demand, in fact

indicators.note: in means the word for demand goes inside the word for fact

parts.note: a deed is a fact, as in 'in deed' meaning in fact
a claim is a demand for something owed

explanation.surface: Something was spoken aloud on demand, as it happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link word; 'in fact' looks like a phrase but 'in' is the container and DEED is fact, as in 'indeed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver a speech or poem in a rhetorical way is to recite it with force.

clue.text: Point about west wind

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for point goes round the compass letter

parts.note: a tine is a point or prong of a fork or antler
W is the compass abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: A compass point near west where the wind blows from.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong thread or string is what one winds, and as a verb it means to coil or twist.

clue.text: Man holds a token

indicators.note: holds means contains, so the name wraps the letter

parts.note: Ernest is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man is holding some token in his hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A payment made as a pledge of more to come is a token of good faith.

clue.text: Maybe the largest — I had one in to try

indicators.note: in means the shortened pronoun and numeral are put inside the word for try

parts.note: to test is to try something out
I'd is the contraction of I had
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Perhaps the biggest is what I had one go at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tidy' is informal British for large, as in 'a tidy sum', so the superlative can mean largest; 'Maybe' marks it as a loose sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A tidy sum is a considerable one, so the most substantial amount is the biggest.
